title: Specialty Insurance Rates Fall Back to 2020 Levels, WTW Survey Finds, as Property and Energy Lead the Softening
summary: WTW's Specialty Insurance Marketplace Survey, reported on May 6, 2026, says its rate index fell 10 points to 2020 levels, with 75% of 42 classes showing decreases at January 1 renewals, while general liability and medical malpractice moved counter-cyclically.
description:
Specialty insurance prices are falling faster than the industry expected. That is the central finding of WTW's Specialty Insurance Marketplace Survey, known as SIMS, reported by Insurance Journal on May 6, 2026. According to the report, rates fell during 2025 and at the January 1, 2026 renewals at a pace that outstripped forecasts by brokers and insurers alike. The survey's rate index dropped 10 points, taking pricing back to the levels last seen in 2020. This article summarises WTW's published findings. An earlier version also said that the January 2026 figures reflected benign catastrophe experience and abundant capacity across all classes; the report ties the benign catastrophe point specifically to property and energy, and that is how it is presented here.

What does the survey cover? WTW says SIMS reflects about $250 billion of gross written premium over a ten-year cycle, including $45 billion in 2025. It spans specialty insurers in London, Bermuda and the US excess and surplus lines (E&S) market. The data comes directly from clients of WTW Insurance Consulting and Technology and is not derived from broker estimates. The global specialty market leader at WTW, Richard Clarkson, is the named spokesperson in the report.

How large is the fall? The report says specialty rates rose about 45% cumulatively between 2017 and the market peak in 2023. Roughly half of that gain has been erased over the past two years. WTW adds that expected 2025 performance, once exposure trends are taken into account, has unwound gains back to 2021 levels. Rates alone are back at 2020 levels. A further sign of competition is that 2025 was the first year since 2018 in which rate adequacy for new business was lower than for renewal business. In practice, this means insurers were prepared to price new customers more aggressively than the customers they already had, a typical sign of insurers competing for share.

How widespread is the softening? According to the report, 75% of the 42 material classes that the survey tracks showed rate decreases at the January 2026 renewals, measured gross of claims trend. A year earlier, the figure was 30%. Aggregate rates fell 5% gross of claims trend and 8% net of claims trend. The net figure adjusts for actuarially estimated claims cost inflation that rate data alone do not capture. In plain terms, once the rising cost of claims is considered, the real price decline is larger than the headline rate change.

Where is it sharpest? Property and energy lines saw the steepest decreases, which WTW attributes to benign catastrophe experience and distorted frequency and severity trends. Marine, financial institutions and professional liability followed. Higher geopolitical tensions partly offset the decline, according to the report. The report does not give class-by-class percentage figures in the version summarised here, so readers who need figures for a particular line should consult the full WTW survey or their broker.

Which lines are going the other way? General liability and medical malpractice are moving counter-cyclically, meaning they are not following the market down. WTW cites substantial concerns about social inflation and nuclear jury verdicts, and also points to expanding litigation funding. Social inflation is the term used for claims costs rising faster than general inflation because of larger court awards and settlements. Nuclear verdicts are jury awards that are extremely large. WTW says it does not believe this trend is sustainable, but acknowledges uncertainty about short-term changes. That wording is important: the firm is describing a risk and a view, not a certain outcome.

What does this mean for buyers? Companies buying specialty cover, such as energy firms, shipowners, banks and professional-services businesses, are generally in a better negotiating position than they were at the peak. Lower rates mean lower costs of risk transfer, and buyers may be able to obtain broader terms or higher limits for the same spend. Buyers in general liability and medical malpractice may not see the same relief.

What does this mean for insurers? The cycle has turned, but the 2017 to 2023 increases mean many insurers entered the softening with strong margins. The question is how far prices fall before returns suffer. WTW's inclusion of claims-trend data is intended to give a fuller view of expected profitability than rate data alone, helping carriers test business plans and assess rate adequacy. The Insurance Journal summary of the report does not include a forecast for mid-year renewals. Investors and regulators will likely watch whether competition on price leads to looser underwriting.

For the wider economy, specialty insurance is the backstop for complex risks. Its pricing cycle affects the cost of building energy projects, moving cargo and running financial institutions. The 2020 level is a useful marker, but it is not a prediction: exposures, claims costs and legal conditions have all changed since then. This article summarises WTW's published survey and is not an investment recommendation or a forecast of future pricing.
source_name: WTW Specialty Insurance Marketplace Survey (via Insurance Journal)

key_points: WTW's SIMS rate index fell 10 points through 2025 and the January 1, 2026 renewals, returning to 2020 levels, faster than brokers and insurers had forecast.
Rates rose about 45% cumulatively from 2017 to the 2023 peak; roughly half of that gain has been erased in two years.
75% of 42 material classes showed rate decreases at January 2026 renewals (gross of claims trend), up from 30% in 2024; aggregate rates fell 5% gross and 8% net of claims trend.
Property and energy saw the steepest decreases, followed by marine, financial institutions and professional liability; general liability and medical malpractice moved counter-cyclically.
The survey covers about $250 billion of gross written premium over a ten-year cycle, including $45 billion in 2025, from London, Bermuda and US excess and surplus lines insurers.
why_it_matters: Specialty insurance covers hard-to-place risks such as energy, marine and professional liability. A fast softening gives buyers lower prices, but it also pressures insurers' margins at a time when WTW warns that litigation costs in liability lines keep rising.

title: Fitch: Japanese and Korean Insurers Are Set to Keep Buying Abroad, With About ¥4.5 Trillion Already Spent and 86% of It in the US
summary: A Fitch Ratings viewpoint of April 29, 2026 says Japanese insurers' major deals total about ¥4.5 trillion (US$35 billion), 86% in the US, and that Korean cross-border M&A reached about $2.6 billion in 2025, with concentration and capital risks to watch.
description:
Insurers in Japan and South Korea are going abroad for growth, and the credit rating agency Fitch expects the shopping to continue. In a viewpoint published by Insurance Journal on April 29, 2026, written by Fitch analysts Teruki Morinaga and Sue Kim, the agency says Japanese and Korean insurers have sharply increased overseas mergers and acquisitions and strategic investments in recent years, in both developed and emerging markets. This article summarises that commentary. An earlier version of this article listed a Mitsui Sumitomo stake in W.R. Berkley and described the Berkshire Hathaway and Tokio Marine partnership as raising Tokio Marine's M&A capacity. Neither point appears in the Fitch text, so they have been removed; the Berkshire partnership is covered in a separate article.

Why are they buying abroad? Fitch points to demographics and slow growth at home. In Japan, the population has declined for 14 consecutive years, which weighs on domestic growth, and Fitch expects Japanese life insurers' underwriting profit margins to peak within five to ten years because of demographic pressure. In Korea, premium growth is slowing because of an ageing population, low economic growth, interest rate cuts and stricter K-ICS capital rules. Fitch projects Korean insurance revenue growth below 5% in 2026. For insurers with large capital bases, buying growth abroad is a response.

The pattern in Japan is established. Fitch says more than half of the Japanese insurers it rates have done M&A in the past decade. Major deals total about ¥4.5 trillion, or about US$35 billion, and 86% of that is in the United States. The agency notes that the US is the only major developed market larger than Japan with steady population growth, and that North America accounts for roughly 40% of global non-life premiums. It lists advantages of the US for Japanese buyers: a familiar business language, transparent corporate law, strong regulation, and the ability to take 100% ownership. It also says Japanese insurers are cash-ready and can outbid private equity buyers. Not every overseas move has worked: Fitch cites Meiji Yasuda's 2023 sale of its stake in PT Avrist Assurance in Indonesia and Dai-ichi's May 2025 plan to divest its stake in Ocean Life Insurance in Thailand as examples of failed Asian deals.

The key deals are named. Tokio Marine entered the US in the early 2000s and has acquired three US insurers. Dai-ichi Life also entered in the early 2000s and acquired Protective Life. Sompo acquired Aspen Insurance Holdings in 2025. Nippon Life announced two acquisitions in 2024, including Resolution Life Group for ¥1.2 trillion, or US$8.4 billion, and is the last major Japanese life insurer to enter North America. Fitch's insurer financial strength ratings for the Japanese groups include AA-/Stable for Tokio Marine & Nichido, Dai-ichi Life and Nippon Life, and A+/Stable for Meiji Yasuda and Sumitomo Life.

The credit effect has been positive so far. Fitch says Japanese insurers target mid-sized US insurers with relatively low credit risk, avoid large natural catastrophe and commodity exposure, and favour specialty lines. Parental support has helped the subsidiaries: Fitch upgraded Resolution Life's US subsidiary, and Protective Life was upgraded two notches to AA-/Stable after Dai-ichi's acquisition. Nearly all Japanese-owned US subsidiaries have performed soundly with steady growth, according to the commentary.

Korea is following, from a smaller base. Korean insurers have historically concentrated on Southeast Asia, such as Vietnam and Indonesia, with minority or strategic stakes. Fitch says cross-border M&A reached about US$2.6 billion in 2025, over 75% of the total M&A value in the past five years. The most active groups are DB Insurance, Samsung Fire & Marine, Hanwha Life and Samsung Life. Hanwha Life acquired 75% of the US brokerage Velocity Clearing in 2025 and 40% of PT Bank Nationalnobu in Indonesia, and DB Insurance acquired Fortegra for US$1.65 billion, which Fitch describes as the first 100% acquisition of a US insurer by a Korean firm and the largest Korean cross-border insurance deal to date. Fitch sees these deals as credit-neutral to mildly positive in the short term, if capital management and integration are prudent.

There are risks. Concentration is the first. Fitch estimates that about 20% of major Japanese life insurers' profits come from North America, with a higher share for non-life insurers: about 60% of Tokio Marine's group income comes from the US, and about 30% of Sompo's, for the fiscal year to March 2025. That makes Japanese insurers more exposed to spillover from US real estate and private credit shocks. Fitch expects more issuance of subordinated bonds to fund acquisitions, particularly by Japanese insurers, since such debt counts as a regulatory capital buffer. In Korea, laws limit insurers' borrowing, so acquisitions are mostly funded from internal liquidity. Fitch estimates that DB Insurance's K-ICS ratio will fall by 15 to 20 percentage points after Fortegra, and that Hanwha Life's ratio fell about 2 points after Velocity. Macroeconomic conditions, geopolitics and regulation could strain buyers and their subsidiaries.

For sellers in the US and Europe, the message is that long-term buyers are available. For customers of acquired companies, the typical pattern is continuity, with the acquired brand and management kept in place. For regulators, the growth of cross-border ownership raises questions about group capital and supervision. This article reports Fitch's views and is not investment advice.
image_alt: Japan Korea insurers global mergers acquisitions cross-border expansion (illustrative)
key_points: Fitch analysts Teruki Morinaga and Sue Kim say Japanese and Korean insurers have sharply increased overseas M&A and expect a strong pipeline, which Fitch sees as broadly credit positive.
More than half of Fitch-rated Japanese insurers have done M&A in the past decade; major deals total about JPY 4.5 trillion (about US$35 billion), 86% of it in the US.
Japan's population has declined for 14 consecutive years and Korean insurance revenue growth is projected below 5% in 2026, pushing both sets of insurers abroad.

Korean cross-border M&A reached about US$2.6 billion in 2025, over 75% of total M&A value in five years; Fitch estimates DB Insurance's K-ICS ratio will fall 15-20% after buying Fortegra for US$1.65 billion.
Concentration is a risk: about 20% of major Japanese life insurers' profits come from North America, around 60% of Tokio Marine's group income comes from the US and about 30% of Sompo's.
why_it_matters: Japan and Korea have ageing populations and slow insurance growth at home. Their insurers' purchases abroad are reshaping the US and European specialty and life markets and could expose them to American credit and real estate shocks.
